history.headline: Thirty-seven deaths confirmed in Willow Street incident
history.text: County dispatch confirmed thirty-seven deaths after a series of white figures entered occupied homes on Willow Street. Doors and windows remained locked. Responders reported that the figures passed through interior walls without damaging them. Several rooms were found empty except for neatly folded clothing and human teeth embedded in the floor. Violet Dunn is among those confirmed dead.

sam.belief: I saw a tall shape beside Reservoir Road. I still can't explain what it was.
sam.stance: I called it The Long Coat. Four people are dead at Harold's store, and I don't care what we call it tonight.

harold.belief: He has not seen the shape and has no firsthand idea what it was.
harold.stance: He prefers The Reservoir Stilt, but has little appetite for arguing over names tonight.

ellen.belief: I have not seen the shape, and I won't pretend otherwise.
ellen.stance: Harold is dead, Vale Hardware is gone, and nine more deaths are confirmed today. A name is beside the point.

turns.text: The bulletin says thirty-seven deaths today. I need to say that plainly. Thirty-seven.
I heard it the first time. I just don't know where to put the number.
You don't put it anywhere. It's the number. That's the awful part.
Violet Dunn is named among the dead. The bulletin says the residential area has been evacuated.
She was a retired teacher. They put that in the notice like the words can hold the rest of it.
They can't. And the description is exact: locked doors, locked windows. The walls weren't damaged.
Responders found rooms empty except for folded clothing and teeth embedded in the floor.
Don't say it like a list. I'm sorry. I know you have to read it. I can't hear it like a list.
There isn't a less terrible way to say it.
No. No, there isn't. The total is forty-four confirmed deaths now.
And I'm still the one people ask to name what I saw. I can't explain it. That doesn't make this any easier.
A name would not tell anyone how to get through a locked house. It would just be another word.
We have no further details from the county bulletin. We don't have a shelter address to give callers.
People are going to want to check on somebody. I understand that. Don't send them back there.
And don't call missing people dead because you are frightened. The confirmed number is already unbearable.
We're staying on the air. If you have a confirmed public notice, call the station. I—I'm sorry. I need to read the bulletin again.
The county says sixty-three people died. I have the line here. I need to keep reading it correctly.
Then say the number. Don't make it smaller by rushing past it.
One hundred seven confirmed deaths in all. Sam Evers is missing. Not confirmed dead.
That distinction matters. It doesn't make the waiting kinder.
The vehicles came back from the opposite direction of travel. They were filled with soil to the windows.
And the people inside had not been on board when they left. That's what the bulletin says. Nothing more.
The eastern highway is gone for two miles. The county calls the replacement surface smooth and warm.
I keep thinking about Sam driving a bus. Now there is a road where the highway was, and he is missing.
The depot is closed. We don't have a passenger list or a shelter address.
Then don't fill the silence with guesses. There are already sixty-three deaths in the announcement.
We have no names for those people. I'm sorry. I keep looking at the bulletin as if another line will appear.
It won't make the number less true.
The station is transmitting recorded material. This Night Line exchange is not live. Ellen Price, what made you call?
I wanted to ask what people are supposed to do for reliable bulletins when the station itself is closed.
You mean the transmitter building is closed, but the station is still broadcasting recordings?
Yes. I heard the bulletin. I don't know where else people can hear a correction if one comes.
Is there a particular correction you are waiting for?
No. I'm asking how a person can tell whether an announcement is current, not whether a rumor is frightening.
What would make it clear to you that it was current?
A date and a source. The bulletin gave a date and said county. Anything less is a voice saying words.
So if someone gives you an instruction without those, you won't pass it on?
I won't pass it on as fact. People hear a confident voice and stop asking who said it.
Has anyone asked you to verify something specific tonight?
No. I'm trying to prevent that from becoming my job just because I work in a library.
The library is closed, too. What can we tell someone who needs a place to check?
I don't know. That's the problem. Don't make up an answer because the question is hard.
Mara Voss, what made you call?
That phrase, “basement recovered.” It sounds as if the contents were recovered. That isn't what the bulletin says.
What's happening on your end—are people asking you about records?
One person asked whether Town Hall's files are safe. I can't answer that from this bulletin.
Did you see the basement yourself?
No. I'm at home. I read the same county wording you did.
So when you say “recovered,” you mean the wording is misleading—not that you have another report?
Yes. It says the basement and utility connections are undamaged. It says nothing about papers.
You said someone asked about files. Did they need a record for something tonight?
They asked if a deed could be checked. I told them I don't know where the records are.
You told them you don't know where the records are. Have you been told they were in the building?
No. I haven't been told anything about the records. I don't know, and I won't turn a guess into an answer.
Can I tell them to call you?
No. I don't know what number you're taking, and I still don't know where they can ask instead.
Oscar Reed, what made you call?
I'm helping with county fair signs. I can't make myself paint the dates on the boards tonight.
What's happening with the signs?
They're stacked in my garage. Nothing happened to them. It's me. I keep hearing nine and staring at the brush.
You said they're in your garage. Are you asking if the fair is canceled?
Yes. I don't know if it is. I need somebody to tell me whether to finish them.
Has anyone from the fair called you?
No. I haven't spoken to them.
So you're waiting on an answer before you paint the dates?
The dates, and the big word WELCOME. I can't write it.
You said you can't write it. Is the board still blank?
No. I started it in pencil. You can see WEL through the paper.
You said it's pencil. Can you turn the board over?
I can. I don't want to. And I still don't know whether to finish the signs.
